DataPropertyAssertion.Literal: Tests for the completion graph caching: each test asks a question whose answer depends on a choice that the consistency test made, and the answer differs from the one that a stale cached model would give. The suite runs every test with the default configuration, with reduced saturation (decision shortcuts off, ABox preparation kept), without completion graph caching (oracle), with reduced saturation and without caching (second oracle), with delayed caching reactivation and without backjumping/semantic branching. Correctness means: all configurations agree and agree with the expected answer.
The ABox of the at-most-nominal-merge family is consistent: a and b are not asserted to be different, so the ontology has a model in which they are the same individual.

o has at most one r-predecessor and a and b are both asserted as r-predecessors of o, so a and b are the same individual. (a and not b) is therefore unsatisfiable. The test merges the test node with the nominal {a}; the cached merge of b into a has to be reactivated and re-derived instead of being taken from the cached model.

Negative control for the nominal merge test: (a and b) is satisfiable because the names may denote the same individual. A reactivation that over-constrains the merged nominal must not make this class unsatisfiable.
a has a t-successor in (K1 or K2), so a may have a K1 t-successor. The class is satisfiable; a cached model that chose K2 must not answer unsatisfiable when the test adds the K1 alternative.

a has at most one t-successor and it is a K1 or a K2, so forbidding a K1 t-successor leaves the K2 alternative and is satisfiable. The test checks that the negated existential is checked against the rebuilt successor instead of the cached label.

Every t-successor of a is a K1 or a K2 (a has exactly one), so forbidding both is unsatisfiable. This is the positive counterpart of the choice tests and fails if the disjunction is not re-applied to the cached successor.
Control: a is not different from itself, so (a and not a) is unsatisfiable for every configuration.
The classifier runs many satisfiability tests on the same cached completion graph. TestNotBoth and TestSelfClash must be classified under owl:Nothing, and TestBoth must stay satisfiable.

OWLlink sequence on one cached graph: TestNotBoth, TestBoth, TestNotBoth, TestSomeK1, TestNoK and TestNotBoth again. The same question has to have the same answer after the other tests, otherwise a test wrote into the shared deterministic or cached graph.

The realizer derives the types of a, b and o from the same cached completion graph: a and b are instances of TestBoth (because they are the same individual) and of owl:Thing, o is an instance of owl:Thing. The realization is the second task type that consumes the cached graph; it must not lose the merged-nominal types.

Four pigeons on three holes force two pigeons onto one hole, so one hole is crowded and the scene is crowded. (Scene and not CrowdedScene) is unsatisfiable. The test merges the scene nominal with the test node, so the hole successors that the cached model merged have to be rebuilt.
Control for the four-pigeons-three-holes case: (Scene and CrowdedScene) is satisfiable, so the reactivation of the merged holes must not introduce a false clash.
Pigeonhole variant in which the holes are linked to the scene by role assertions: (Scene and not CrowdedScene) is unsatisfiable because the pigeon choices force a crowded hole.
Control for the role-assertion pigeonhole variant: (Scene and CrowdedScene) is satisfiable.

Negative control for the pigeonhole family: two pigeons on two holes need not share a hole, so (Scene and not CrowdedScene) is satisfiable. A reactivation that rebuilds too much must not produce a false clash here.
Classification of the four-pigeons-three-holes ontology: Scene and CrowdedScene are equivalent and TestSceneNotCrowded is unsatisfiable. The classifier runs the tests on the same cached graph.
OWLlink sequence of issue #19 on one cached graph: the same unsatisfiability question is asked twice, interrupted by other tests and by a subsumption test. The repeated answers must not change.
The disjunction family is consistent: a chooses one of C1 and C2 and the respective D is propagated to o.
Whichever disjunct a takes, it forces D1 or D2 onto its r-successor o, so (o and not D1 and not D2) is unsatisfiable. The test touches the cached neighbour of the disjunction decision.
a is a C1 or a C2, so a itself is a D1 or a D2; forbidding both is unsatisfiable.
o is a D2; a has to take C2. If the cached model chose C1 (which forces D1 onto o and D1 is disjoint from D2), the choice has to be given up; a stale cached choice would answer unsatisfiable.
o is a D1; the C1 alternative satisfies the ontology, so the class is satisfiable.
D1 and D2 are disjoint, so (o and D1 and D2) is unsatisfiable.
a is not a D1: the C2 alternative is still open, so this is satisfiable and must not inherit the cached D1 from a C1 model.
o is a D1 and not a D2, so the C2 alternative is impossible and a has to take C1; the class is satisfiable, which fails if the reactivated disjunction is not decided again.
Classification of the disjunction family: TestONoBranch and TestANoBranch must be under owl:Nothing, and the satisfiable test classes must not be.
The at-most-merge family is consistent: the two r-successors of a are merged into one node that is a B1 and a B2.

a has at most one r-successor and requires one in B1 and one in B2, so the only successor is a B1 and a B2. (a and not (some r (B1 and B2))) is unsatisfiable; it is the criterion C8/C4 shape for blockable successors.
Control: (a and some r (B1 and B2)) is satisfiable because the two required successors are merged.
There is exactly one r-successor and it is a B1 and a B2, so (a and all r (B1 and B2)) is satisfiable.
a requires an r-successor in B1, so (a and not (some r B1)) is unsatisfiable.
a has an r-successor in B1, so not every r-successor is a non-B1; (a and not (all r B1)) is unsatisfiable.
Control: (a and some r B1 and some r B2) is satisfiable with one merged successor for both existentials.
a requires an r-successor, so (a and at most 0 r) is unsatisfiable.
The t-successor of a is a K1 or a K2, so forbidding both is unsatisfiable. This is the second non-deterministic choice of the family; it has to be re-decided after the r-successors were merged.
Control: a may have a K2 t-successor, so (a and some t K2) is satisfiable.
Classification of the at-most-merge family: the unsatisfiable test classes must be under owl:Nothing while the control classes stay satisfiable.
The qualified at-most family is consistent: a has one C-successor that is a D1, and o has one C-predecessor, namely a.

a already has one C-successor that is a D1, and D1 and D2 are disjoint. A second C-successor in D2 either merges with the existing one (D1 against D2) or exceeds the qualified at-most restriction of a; the class is unsatisfiable. The new successor is not in the cached model, so C4 has to count it.
Control: the existing C-successor is a D1, so (a and some r (C and D1)) is satisfiable.
The qualified restriction counts only C-successors, so an additional non-C r-successor is allowed and (a and some r (not C)) is satisfiable.
Control: (a and some r (C and not C)) is unsatisfiable, independent of the caching.

o has at most one C-predecessor through the inverse role and a is such a predecessor. A new predecessor that is a C and a D2 is distinct from a (a is a D1), so it violates the inverse at-most restriction; the class is unsatisfiable. This checks C4 for a new nominal neighbour.
Control: the one C-predecessor of o is a and a is a D1, so (o and some inv(r) (C and D1)) is satisfiable.
A D2 predecessor need not be a C, so it is not counted by the qualified inverse at-most restriction and (o and some inv(r) D2) is satisfiable.
a is a C and an r-predecessor of o, so (o and all inv(r) (not C)) is unsatisfiable.
Control: with an at-most of two C-successors the single existing one is allowed, so the class is satisfiable.
a requires a C-successor in D1, so (a and not (some r (C and D1))) is unsatisfiable.
Classification of the qualified at-most family: the unsatisfiable test classes must be under owl:Nothing and the controls must stay satisfiable.
The inverse-GCI family is consistent: o chooses B1 or B2 and the corresponding D is derived for a.
o is a B1 or a B2, and the normalised inverse existentials derive D1 or D2 for a. (a and not D1 and not D2) is unsatisfiable; the cached ALL concept has to reach the rebuilt inverse successor of a.
a is not a D1: o may choose B2 and derive D2, so the class is satisfiable. A cached model that chose B1 must give the choice up.
Symmetric re-choice test: a is not a D2, so o may choose B1 and derive D1.
Control: (a and D1) is satisfiable with o being a B1.
Control: (a and D1 and D2) is satisfiable because D1 and D2 do not exclude each other.
o is a B1 or a B2, so forbidding both is unsatisfiable.
Control: o may be a B2, so (o and not B1) is satisfiable.
a has o as an inverse-r-successor and o is a B1 or a B2, so (a and not (some inv(r) B1) and not (some inv(r) B2)) is unsatisfiable.
Control: (a and not (some inv(r) B1)) is satisfiable with o being a B2.
o is the only inverse-r-successor of a and it is a B1 or a B2, so (a and all inv(r) (not B1) and all inv(r) (not B2)) is unsatisfiable.
Control: o may be a B1, so (o and not B2) is satisfiable.
Classification of the inverse-GCI family: TestANoBranch and TestONoBranch must be under owl:Nothing, the re-choice controls stay satisfiable.

OWLlink sequence on one cached graph: TestANoBranch, TestANotD1 twice, TestANoBranch again and TestONoBranch. A changed answer of the repeated questions indicates a write into the shared cached graph.
Control for the negative pigeonhole case: (Scene and CrowdedScene) is satisfiable when two pigeons sit on two holes.
Classification of the role-assertion pigeonhole variant: Scene and CrowdedScene are equivalent and TestSceneNotCrowded is unsatisfiable.
The ABox with twelve independent groups is consistent: in every group the two r-predecessors of o_i are the same individual.

In group 5, o_5 has at most one r-predecessor and both a_5 and b_5 are predecessors, so (a_5 and not b_5) is unsatisfiable. The test merges the test node with the nominal a_5 in a large ABox whose other groups must keep their cached state.
Control for group 5: (a_5 and b_5) is satisfiable because the two names may denote the same individual.
Same merge test for group 9: the reactivation has to find b_9 without rebuilding the unrelated groups.
Same merge test for the last group: it touches the group that the individual saturation processes last.
The reverse nominal order of the merge test: (b_1 and not a_1) is unsatisfiable for the same reason as (a_1 and not b_1).
The t-successor of a_1 is a K1 or a K2, so forbidding both is unsatisfiable. The choice sits in the first group of a large ABox.
Control for the choice in the large ABox: (a_1 and not (some t K1)) is satisfiable because a_1 may choose K2.
Control: a_3 is an r-predecessor of o_3, so (o_3 and some inv(r) {a_3}) is satisfiable.
Classification over the large ABox: the merge test classes and the choice test classes must be placed under owl:Nothing, the controls must stay satisfiable.

The realizer derives the types of every individual of the large ABox from the cached completion graph. All a_i, b_i and o_i are instances of owl:Thing; the merge of each pair must not remove an individual from the result.
The data value family is consistent: o has one of the two disjunctive values and the universal restriction of a excludes the value 1.

o is a d-value 1 or 2 and the universal restriction of a excludes the value 1, so o has to be 2; (o and not (d = 2)) is unsatisfiable. The cached node has a data label that has to be re-derived after the test node was merged with {o}.
Control: (o and (d = 2)) is satisfiable because o is forced to the value 2.
Control: (o and not (d = 1)) is satisfiable because o is forced to the value 2.
The functional data property forbids two different values, so (o and (d = 1)) contradicts the forced value 2 and is unsatisfiable.
(o and (d = 1) and (d = 2)) is unsatisfiable because the data property is functional and the two values are different.
o is a value 1 or a value 2, so forbidding both is unsatisfiable. The disjunction of the data has-value restrictions is the cached choice.
Control: the value of o is in the data range {1, 2}, so the existential restriction is satisfiable.
Every value of o is 1 or 2, so no value is outside {1, 2} and the negated existential is unsatisfiable.
Every r-successor of a is not a d-value 1, so (a and some r (d = 1)) is unsatisfiable.
Control: the only r-successor of a is o and o is forced to 2, so (a and some r (d = 2)) is satisfiable.
The only r-successor of a is o with the forced value 2, so (a and some r (not (d = 2))) is unsatisfiable.
Classification of the data value family: the unsatisfiable value test classes must be under owl:Nothing and the value controls stay satisfiable.
The rule family is consistent: the named individual k is a K1 or a K2, and the rule corresponding to the chosen alternative derives M or N on the named individual l.

k is the named individual that is a K1 or a K2 and t(k,l) links it to the named individual l. In the K1 alternative the rule derives M on every t-successor of k, in the K2 alternative it derives N; (l and not M and not N) is therefore unsatisfiable. DL-safe rules fire on named individuals only, so this is the caching-relevant shape: the rule binding depends on the cached choice for the nominal k and has to be re-derived when that choice is redone.
Control: choosing K1 derives M on l, so (l and M) is satisfiable.
Control: choosing K2 derives N on l, so (l and N) is satisfiable.
Choosing K2 leaves l without M, so (l and not M) is satisfiable. A rule binding from a cached K1 choice must be given up and must not derive M.
Symmetric control: choosing K1 leaves l without N.
Control: k may be a K2, so (k and not K1) is satisfiable.
k is a K1 or a K2, so forbidding both is unsatisfiable.

The role hierarchy family is consistent: the sub-role successors of a are merged by the at-most restriction on the super-role r, the transitive and the chain links are asserted consistently, and i and j are the same individual.

The r1-successor in B1 and the r2-successor in B2 are both r-successors and a has at most one, so they are merged into a B1/B2 node. (a and not (some r (B1 and B2))) is unsatisfiable; the r-successor is counted through the super-role of the two asserted sub-roles.
After the merge the surviving node is still reachable through r1, so (a and not (some r1 (B1 and B2))) is unsatisfiable. This is the cached-neighbour criterion C8 through a sub-role.
The symmetric sub-role test: the merged node is also reachable through r2, so (a and not (some r2 (B1 and B2))) is unsatisfiable.
a requires an r1-successor in B1, so (a and not (some r1 B1)) is unsatisfiable.
a has r-successors, so (a and at most 0 r) is unsatisfiable.

t is transitive, t(c,d), t(d,e) and every t-successor of c is a C, so C(e) holds and (e and not C) is unsatisfiable. The test depends on the cached transitive link that the completion has to re-derive.
t(c,d) and every t-successor of c is a C, so (d and not C) is unsatisfiable.
The transitive closure of t links c to e, so (e and not (some inv(t) {c})) is unsatisfiable.
The chain t1 o t2 is a sub-property of s and links f to h, so (h and not (some inv(s) {f})) is unsatisfiable. The chain automaton has to be re-applied to the cached links.
Control: the chain derives the s-link from f to h, so (f and some s {h}) is satisfiable.
o3 has at most one r-predecessor; r1(i,o3) and r2(j,o3) are two r-predecessors because r1 and r2 are sub-roles of r, so i and j are the same individual and (i and not j) is unsatisfiable.
Control: (i and j) is satisfiable because the two sub-role predecessors may be the same individual.
Classification of the role hierarchy family: the unsatisfiable sub-role, transitivity and chain test classes must be under owl:Nothing and the controls stay satisfiable.
OWLlink sequence on one cached graph: TestNoMergedSuccessor, TestMergedR1, TestNoMergedSuccessor again, TestChainLink and TestSubroleMerge. The repeated question must keep its answer.
The cyclic blocking family is consistent: the A-node chain is blocked and every node chooses C1 or C2.
A is a subclass of (some r A) and a is an A, so (a and not (some r A)) is unsatisfiable.
Every r-successor of a is an A and therefore a C1 or a C2, so (a and not (some r (C1 or C2))) is unsatisfiable.
Every r-successor is an A and therefore a C1 or a C2, so forbidding C1 and C2 on all r-successors is unsatisfiable. The universal restrictions have to be applied to the blocked successors as well.
Control: choosing C2 at a and along the blocked chain leaves no C1 successor, so the class is satisfiable.
Control: choosing C1 at a and along the blocked chain leaves no C2 successor.
Control: choosing C1 at a and on every successor satisfies (a and all r C1).
Control: choosing C2 at a and on every successor satisfies (a and all r C2).
Control: the successor of a may be a C1, so (a and some r C1) is satisfiable.
a is an A and therefore a C1 or a C2, so (a and not (C1 or C2)) is unsatisfiable.
Every r-successor of a is an A, so (a and all r (not A)) is unsatisfiable.
Classification of the cyclic blocking family: the unsatisfiable test classes must be under owl:Nothing and the control classes stay satisfiable.

The six-pigeons-five-holes family is consistent: the pigeons choose holes, one hole has to hold two pigeons, and the data value choice and the role chain are satisfiable together with the nominal merges.

Six distinct pigeons on five distinct holes force one hole onto two pigeons, so that hole is a CrowdedHole and the scene is a CrowdedScene; (Scene and not CrowdedScene) is unsatisfiable. The instance is larger than family B, combines the data value choice and a chain on the same model, and every pigeon/hole choice is on the same cached graph.
Control: (Scene and CrowdedScene) is satisfiable for the six-pigeons-five-holes instance; a reactivation that rebuilds too much must not turn it unsatisfiable.

Every pigeon has the value 1 or the value 2 of the functional data property, so ({p0} and not (d = 1) and not (d = 2)) is unsatisfiable. The data label of a pigeon that was merged during the pigeonhole assignment has to be re-derived.
Control: ({p0} and (d = 1)) is satisfiable because the value choice is open.

p0 sits on a hole and every hole is in the scene; the role chain sitsAt o inScene is a sub-property of locatedIn, so p0 is locatedIn s and ({p0} and not (some locatedIn {s})) is unsatisfiable. The chain link has to be re-derived on the cached successors.
Control: the six pigeons can be distributed as 2,1,1,1,1, so a particular hole such as h0 need not be crowded; (h0 and not CrowdedHole) is satisfiable.

Classification of the six-pigeons-five-holes instance: Scene and CrowdedScene are equivalent, TestSceneNotCrowded, TestValueChoice and TestNoLocatedIn are under owl:Nothing, TestSceneCrowded and TestValueOne are satisfiable.
The exact-cardinality variant is consistent: A is {a0,a1}, B is {a0,a4}, and B has exactly two B-successors.

The exact cardinality two forces both B-instances to be r-successors of every B-instance, including the self loop of a4. The disjointness then forces a4 into A and a4 = a1, so (A and not B) is unsatisfiable. The at-most part of the exact cardinality is the additional shape compared with the minimum-cardinality family.
The same forced equality from the nominal side: ({a1} and not {a4}) is unsatisfiable because a1 = a4 in every model.
Symmetric nominal test: ({a4} and not {a1}) is unsatisfiable for the same forced equality.
Control: ({a1} and {a4}) is satisfiable because a1 and a4 are the same individual.
The three-instance complete-graph variant is consistent: A is {a0,a1,a2}, B is {a0,a4,a5}, and every B-instance has three distinct B-successors (a0, a4, a5).

Three distinct B-successors among the three B-instances force a0, a4 and a5 to be distinct and mutually r-related. The disjointness forces a4 and a5 into A; they are distinct and not a0, so they are a1 and a2 and A = B. (A and not B) is unsatisfiable. The complete graph has more blocked and merged nodes than the two-instance family.
({a1} and not {a2}) is satisfiable: a1 and a2 are distinct because a4 and a5 are two distinct A-elements besides a0. The test distinguishes the forced equality from a false merge of all nominals.
Control: ({a4} and {a1}) is satisfiable because a4 can be a1 (the other A-element is a2).
Control: A is satisfiable (it has three instances in every model).
The no-disjointness control is consistent: a4 may be a C, so no equality with a1 is forced.
Control for over-reactivation: without C disjoint D, a4 may be a C (and a D), so A and B need not be equal and (A and not B) is satisfiable. Waking the blocked nodes must not force the equality.
Control: ({a1} and not {a4}) is satisfiable when a4 may be a C, so a1 and a4 can be different individuals.
Control: ({a1} and {a4}) is still satisfiable in the branch where a4 chooses A.
Control: a4 can be a C outside A, so ({a4} and not A) is satisfiable.
Classification of the no-disjointness control: A and B are not equivalent and none of the four test classes is under owl:Nothing.
